newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault's survival at stake - minister.
newsitem.headline: Renault's survival at stake - minister.

text.p: French Industry Minister Franck Borotra on Tuesday defended carmaker Renault's plans to cut nearly 6,000 jobs in Europe, saying its survival was at stake.
"You talk to me about a strategy of job-cutting. The strategy at stake here is the strategy of survival for the company," Borotra told Parliament during weekly questions.

He blasted what he called the European Commission's double-standard regarding Renault's actions. "When JVC relocated out of Lorraine, when Hoover pulled out of Bourgogne, when Grundig closed down its Creutzvald activities, I don't recall getting support from the European Commission," Borotra said.
"I remember the (French) government standing alone to defend the future of these industries and their workers," he said.
"If we're going to talk about a social Europe, we need to fight against social dumping, subsidy-chasing and competitive devaluations...which caused considerable harm to our car sector," he said.
The weakness of the dollar and sterling in 1995 and 1996 and the devaluation of the Italian lira were hugely disadvantageous to Renault and its French rival PSA Peugeot Citroen.

Borotra spoke after more than 7,000 people, mostly Renault workers from France and Belgium, demonstrated in Paris against Renault's plans to close the Vilvoorde plant in Belgium and eliminate 2,764 jobs this year in France.

"Workers are worried, and I too am worried about the future of the European car industry," he said. "I'd like us to sit down with the car manufacturers and look at not just the industrial restructuring needed but also at the social consequences and all the factors relating to the competitiveness of these companies."
Borotra said the industry faced a major challenge at the turn of the century.

Voluntary quotas limiting Japanese car exports to Europe will end in the year 2,000. Korean carmakers are also making rapid inroads into the slow-growing European market, which is plagued by overcapacity estimated at 20 percent or more.

Renault, the smallest of Europe's six volume manufacturers, is expected next week to announce a net loss of between five and six billion francs ($870.6 million and $1 billion) for 1996, including restructuring charges.
